prompt: Two cylindrical soup cans are similar (the same shape, different sizes). The small can is $3$ in tall and the large can is $5$ in tall. What is the ratio of the small can's volume to the large can's volume?
hint: For similar solids: lengths scale by $k$, surface areas by $k^2$, volumes by $k^3$.

hints.text: For similar solids: lengths scale by $k$, surface areas by $k^2$, volumes by $k^3$.

hints.title: 🪜 Try a simpler one
hints.text: See it on cubes: a $1$ by $1$ by $1$ cube holds $1$ and a $2$ by $2$ by $2$ cube holds $8$ — lengths $1 : 2$ but volumes $1 : 8$, the ratio cubed. Do the same cubing to $3 : 5$.
Here $k = \frac{3}{5}$, and volume needs the cube.
$\left(\frac{3}{5}\right)^3 = \frac{27}{125}$, so the ratio is $27 : 125$. Choice C.

explanation: Similar solids have all matching lengths in the same ratio, here $3 : 5$.
Volume is a three-dimensional measure, so it scales by the cube of that ratio.

alternativeExplanations.title: Check it with real numbers
steps: Say the small can has radius $3$ and height $3$: $V = \pi(9)(3) = 27\pi$.
The similar large can has radius $5$ and height $5$: $V = \pi(25)(5) = 125\pi$. The ratio is $27\pi : 125\pi = 27 : 125$ ✓

alternativeExplanations.title: ⚠️ The trap here
steps: Choice A, $3 : 5$, is the trap: assuming volume scales the same way length does. It does not — the large can is not merely $\frac{5}{3}$ as roomy, it is more than four times as roomy.
Ask what KIND of measure the question wants: a length uses $k$, an area (paint, labels, wrapping) uses $k^2$, a volume (soup, water, sand) uses $k^3$. Soup fills space, so cube it.
